headline: Little Egg Reef Fluke Hold on the Slack, Bunker Tightens the Inlet Cuts
subhead: The full moon tide did what we said it would to the bait — now the question is whether the bass commit before the new moon on the 10th.
body_markdown:
The cut on the north end of Holgate hasn't moved much since late August, and that's worth paying attention to. It's the same trough that scoured out during that run of southwest wind a few weeks back — still a good eighteen inches to two feet deeper than the surrounding sandbar, still funneling current hard on the outgoing, and it's been holding peanut bunker and rain bait every tide change since. When a cut sits stable like that through a full moon cycle, it tells you the bottom's found its shape for the season. That's the kind of structure you build a week around, not just a tide.

Speaking of the moon — Saturday's full moon did exactly what we flagged it would. Bait schools from Little Egg Inlet down through Great Bay tightened up hard behind it, and the bass that had been picking at stragglers all week started showing real intent on peanut bunker and spot staged tight to the inlet mouths. That's the pattern building right now, and if it holds, the new moon on the 10th is shaping up to be the real trigger for the first legitimate fall blitz activity on this stretch. We're not there yet. But the ingredients are stacking the way they're supposed to.

Fluke are still the more reliable player through the middle of this week, even as the calendar starts working against them. Little Egg Reef has been loaded — mostly shorts mixed in with a solid percentage of keepers, coming on spearing and squid strips fished on standard fluke rigs in 20 to 30 feet. The keeper ratio is better on the last two hours of the incoming into the first hour of high, when the current slows enough for the bait to sit still instead of getting swept off bottom. Back on the flats — Graveling Point, the edges of the Mullica channel, and the skinny water off Great Bay — bucktail and Gulp combos are still drawing strikes on the dropping tide, white and pink 3-inch Swimming Mullets on 3/8-ounce bucktails working best for anglers dragging slow across the mussel bars. That bite is going to keep tapering through the week as water temps ease back and fluke start staging for their fall pullout. If fluke is the priority, this week and maybe next is the window — don't wait on it.

Striper interest is real but still building, not exploding. Live spot and peanut bunker fished on fish-finder rigs at the mouth of Little Egg Inlet and along the Barnegat Light jetty rocks have been picking up slot fish on the last of the outgoing, when bait gets flushed out of the back bay and funnels past the rocks. Surfcasters working the Holgate cut at first light have had better luck with bunker-colored darters and swimming plugs worked slow through that deeper trough than with anything fished fast — these early-season bass are still keying on wounded, disoriented bait, not chasing hard. Nothing blitz-worthy yet. Think one or two fish a tide for those putting in the time at the right stage of water, mostly in the 26 to 32-inch range with an occasional bigger fish mixed in around the inlet structure itself. That's honest work right now, not a sure thing.

Bluefish are the wild card worth watching closer than usual. As the tides build toward Thursday's new moon, bunker schools pushing through Little Egg Inlet and staging off Beach Haven are starting to draw serious blue interest — birds working bait pods just outside the inlet mouth on the last two days have been a tip-off. Metal — Kastmasters and Deadly Dicks in the 1 to 2-ounce range — worked fast through the edges of those bunker schools has been the go-to, and there's no reason that shouldn't hold or improve as the tide range increases through the week.

Weakfish and kingfish haven't shown much of a pattern worth reporting on yet this week — both are still around in the back bay in small numbers, but nothing concentrated enough to chase specifically. Black drum season on this stretch is essentially closed out for the year at this point; that window was spring.

Looking at the next few days: expect the fluke bite to stay steady but keep sliding as the week goes on, so if Little Egg Reef or the back bay flats are the plan, sooner is better than later. The bigger story is what happens between now and the new moon on the 10th. If the bunker schools keep tightening the way they have been — and there's no reason to think they won't with this tide building — the first real blitz window of the fall should open up somewhere between Little Egg Inlet and the Barnegat Light rocks in the next seven to ten days. Watch for diving birds and nervous water on the outgoing, especially in that first hour after the tide turns, when bait gets squeezed hard against the jetty rocks and the cuts. That's where this is headed. It's not here yet, but the setup is about as clean as it gets this time of year.
